content:
Facts A forced heir challenged testamentary dispositions and inter vivos donations made by her parents, alleging infringement of her reserved share and seeking reduction, restitution, and division of several estates; multiple preliminary objections and partial judgments had become final.
Legal framework
Articles 542, 556, 560, 581, 588, 654, 720, 752 ICC on reserved shares, fictitious reconstitution, reduction, institutio ex re certa, partial ineffectiveness of wills, division and reimbursement of estate expenses; Articles 324, 2909 ICC and 190, 720, 788 CPC; settled Supreme Court case law on burden of proof in reduction actions.
Interpretative issue
Whether an action for reduction is admissible and well-founded when the claimant generically alleges infringement of the reserved share without precisely determining the value of the estate and the extent of the alleged lesion, and whether reduction may be claimed individually by a co-heir.
Principle applied
In actions for reduction, the forced heir bears the burden of specifically alleging and proving the value of the estate, the fictitious reconstitution under Article 556 ICC, and the exact extent of the infringement of the reserved share, as well as expressly seeking reinstatement. Generic allegations of a “probable” lesion are insufficient and lead to dismissal. The action for reduction is strictly personal and cannot be exercised to vindicate the reserved shares of other co-heirs. Testamentary provisions referring to non-existent assets entail only partial ineffectiveness, not invalidity of the will. Where no infringement is established, claims for reduction are rejected, while residual claims for division of an intestate estate are governed by ordinary rules on divisibility in kind and cash adjustments.
